source: web research by MOSE research agents; every claim traced to a listed source. Verify anything you act on.

firms.name: Bill Ackman — Pershing Square (Pershing Square Capital Management, L.P. / Pershing Square Inc.)
firms.who: Bill Ackman, founder (2004), New York. Concentrated long-only-ish activist and quality investor: ~11–15 large positions, multi-year holds, occasional index/credit hedges. The listed vehicle Pershing Square Holdings (PSH, London/Euronext) holds the book; the management company Pershing Square Inc. went public in 2026 (final prospectus on file). 13F filings moved from the fund CIK 1336528 to the holdco 2026053 mid-2026 — MOSE merges both. Regulatory AUM ~$25B; Q2 2026 13F book $19.5B, 15 positions, top-10 ~93%, quarterly turnover ~16%.
firms.terms: PSH: 1.5% management + 16% incentive, trades on the LSE/Euronext at a discount to NAV — the one way a retail investor can literally own Ackman's book. The private funds are closed.
firms.track_record: Jan 2004–Dec 2025: 16.2% compounded NAV return vs S&P 10.7%. 2025: NAV +20.9%, shareholder return +33.9% as the discount narrowed (S&P +17.9%). 2026: Q1 drawdown of −13.9%; NAV −3.4% YTD at 25 Aug vs S&P roughly +14%. 13F-clone over the last two years: −5.9% vs SPY +19.5% — the lag and the position changes cost the copier. Big historic wins: MBIA short, General Growth (2009), Canadian Pacific, Chipotle, the 2020 CDS hedge ($27M → $2.6B). Big losses: Valeant (~−$4B, 2015–17), the Herbalife short (~−$1B, 2012–18).
firms.good: One of the few managers whose largest positions are genuinely large — 10–20% each — so the 13F carries real conviction. The book is now almost entirely Joe's own list: Uber, Brookfield, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Restaurant Brands, Howard Hughes, and new in Q2 2026 Visa, Mastercard, S&P Global ($1.1B each), Netflix ($934M), ICE, Alcon. Communicates constantly; the Q2 letter and annual report are detailed.
firms.bad: Fast for a 'long-term' investor: fully exited Alphabet in Q2 2026 (to fund a $2.4B Microsoft stake), cut Amazon ~25%, sold Universal Music after a rejected bid. Turnover ~16%/q plus a taste for reversals means the 45-day lag matters. Returned to Netflix after a losing 2022 round-trip. 2026 is running well behind the index.
firms.ugly: Valeant: a ~$4B loss defended publicly for two years. Herbalife: a five-year public short that lost ~$1B. Pershing Square Tontine (the largest-ever SPAC) unwound in 2022 and returned $4B; the Pershing Square USA IPO was pulled in 2024 after targets fell from $25B to ~$2B. He is loud on X and politics, and his calls move his own stocks. Howard Hughes: the Q2 13F shows it still in the book (~7%) even though headlines said 'exits' — the position moved between the fund and the holdco, which is why MOSE tracks both CIKs.
firms.how_to_engage: Buy PSH on the London Stock Exchange (or the OTC line PSHZF) — a listed closed-end fund at a discount to NAV. That is the only route; the private funds are closed.
firms.mose_note: Recommendation: Bench, with a real case for Core. His book IS Joe's buy list at conviction sizes, which is the argument for Core; the turnover, the reversals and the activist theatre are the argument against. If Joe wants one activist in Core, this is the one.

firms.name: David Rolfe — Wedgewood Partners
firms.who: David Rolfe, CIO since 1992, St. Louis. Employee-owned, founded 1988. 'Focused growth': ~20 stocks, quality growth bought at a reasonable price, multi-year holds — the Munger wing. Runs separate accounts and the Wedgewood Fund (via RiverPark). Regulatory AUM ~$561M; 13F book $484M, 18–22 positions, top-10 ~64%, turnover ~9%/q, median hold 8 quarters. Open to individual clients (186 individual / 145 high-net-worth accounts on the ADV).
firms.terms: Separate accounts (SMA) — genuinely accessible. Fee schedule not disclosed on the ADV extract; phone 314-567-6407, wedgewoodpartners.com.
firms.track_record: Since 1992: about 11.4% a year net (13.1% gross) vs S&P ~9.7% — a 30-year beat. But the firm went from ~$4B (2019) to ~$0.5B today: the 2017–2020 stretch badly trailed the index and clients left. 13F-clone over the last two years: +1.8% vs SPY +19.5%. Last-12-month return about +12%.
firms.good: Long, honest, public record; quarterly letters are among the most candid in the business (he names his mistakes). Book today: TSM 10%, GOOGL 9%, META 9%, AAPL 8%, MSFT 7%, AMZN 7%, V 6%, Motorola Solutions, Old Dominion, Booking — almost a mirror of Joe's Forever + Toll booths.
firms.bad: Small now. A $500M shop with 300 client accounts is a boutique, and its 13F moves are tiny in dollars. The 2017–2020 underperformance was real and long.
firms.ugly: Sold Berkshire Hathaway in 2019 after ~20 years, publicly calling Buffett's cash pile 'a considerable impediment of growth' — right before Berkshire's strong 2021–24. Assets fell roughly 85% from peak as clients redeemed. No regulatory flags (ADV disclosure count 0).
firms.how_to_engage: Direct SMA client. Call the St. Louis office; ask for the fee schedule and minimum. One of the few Core-quality managers on the roster Joe could actually hire.
firms.mose_note: Recommendation: Core. Right school, long record, low turnover, book overlaps Joe's list almost exactly. Small size is the only knock and it doesn't affect the vote.

firms.name: Saybrook Capital — Scott Hirsch & Luke Babcock
firms.who: Independent investment counsel, Winston-Salem NC (SEC name 'SAYBROOK CAPITAL /NC'; offices also in Sag Harbor and New York, which is why the filing shows NY). Founded 1976; owned and run by Scott Hirsch and Luke Babcock, both value-trained. Small staff, individual and family clients. 13F book $371M, 42 positions, top-10 ~74%, turnover ~7%/q, median hold 8 quarters. MOSE's Form ADV join missed it (name mismatch) — it IS a registered adviser; Form CRS on file.
firms.terms: Fee-only SMA: percentage of assets, billed quarterly — the brochure's example is $12,500 a year on $1M (1.25%). No minimum stated.
firms.track_record: No published composite found. 13F-implied 2-year return +16.0%; 13F-clone +6.2% vs SPY +19.5%. Book is stable quarter to quarter: Alphabet (both classes) ~27%, Berkshire ~17%, Apple ~11%, Visa 5%, Sherwin-Williams 5%, ADP, RTX, FactSet, Norfolk Southern, Honeywell.
firms.good: Fifty-year-old firm with a stated 'undervalued growth' discipline: quality, sustainable advantage, low debt, ethical management, buy only when undervalued. Very low turnover. Top three positions are Joe's top three.
firms.bad: It is a two-partner wealth-management shop, not a fund with a track record you can audit. Alphabet + Berkshire + Apple at ~55% of the book means its 'vote' is mostly a vote for three stocks Joe already owns. 42 positions with a long tail.
firms.ugly: Nothing found — no regulatory actions, no blow-ups, no press. The absence of any public record is itself the caveat: you are trusting a discipline you cannot verify beyond the filings.
firms.how_to_engage: saybrookcapital.com; Winston-Salem office. SMA client at ~1.25%.
firms.mose_note: Recommendation: Bench. Right philosophy, clean, but unverifiable and its vote is concentrated in three names Joe already holds at the top of consensus. Core would double-count what he already has.
